blocks.text: When her people confront Maryam ﵍ with her infant, the Qur'an gives their address, the sister of Aaron, joined to a defense of her parents' honor (Qur'an 19:27-28). Aaron the prophet, brother of Moses ﵇, lived about a thousand years before her. Christian critics say the Qur'an has confused two women, Maryam ﵍ the mother of Isa ﵇ and Miriam the sister of Moses ﵇, and rolled them into one. If she was not Aaron's ﵇ sister, the charge concludes, the verse should never have said sister.

blocks.text: The surah's own story answers the family questions in order. Her father was Imran, her mother Hanna. Her mother vowed the child in her womb to the sanctuary, the custodians cast lots for her care, and the lot fell to Zakariyya ﵇, the husband of her sister. Her father is not the Amram who fathered Moses ﵇ and Aaron ﵇ a thousand years earlier; the two men share one ancient name, carried by the custom of naming children after the righteous. Sister of Aaron rides the same custom and the language's kinship grammar. The school's recorded readings, the Prophet's ﷺ own answer at Najran, the lexicons, the poetry they preserve, and the Gospel's kinship words all carry it.

blocks.text: The Imams ﵈, the twelve of the Ahl al-Bayt whom the school follows, read the verse this way from the beginning. Ali ibn Ibrahim al-Qummi (d.329) narrates the scene and explains the address inside it. Al-Sharif al-Murtada (d.436) gave a session of his Amali to the readings of the verse. The objection reached the Prophet ﷺ in his own lifetime from the Christians of Najran, and his answer has chains in the Sunni and the Shia books alike.

Al-Hilli (d.726) names the couple the same way (Idah al-Mukhalafa, p.204). The Qur'an opens her birth story with this woman's vow (Qur'an 3:35) and calls Maryam the daughter of Imran (Qur'an 66:12), naming the man of her own century.

A woman of Aaron's ﵇ line, stated by al-Murtada among the readings and carried by Muqatil from the Prophet ﷺ. A righteous brother who shared neither of her parents. On none of them does the verse name a womb-sister of Moses' ﵇ brother, and that is the only reading the confusion charge needs.

The Children of Israel used to attach their children to their prophets and righteous men, and an address by a saint's name follows that custom. blocks.text: Al-Murtada's Amali keeps the exchange in the school's own sitting, where the Prophet's ﷺ rebuke is softened into a lesson. When the Messenger of Allah sent al-Mughira to the people of Najran, they said his Prophet claimed Aaron was the brother of Moses ﵇, when Allah knows the years between Moses and Jesus. Al-Mughira did not know what to answer until he returned. The Prophet ﷺ asked him why he had not said that they used to name themselves after their prophets and the righteous before them (al-Murtada, Amali, vol.2, p.197). Al-Mughira was silent on the spot, and the answer he carried back named a custom checkable in the objectors' own scripture.

blocks.text: On this reading the crowd named no genealogy of hers. They cut her with a comparison to a notorious man of their own generation, a Harun known for sin. The address is an insult, and an insult needs a reference the audience shares. A Harun of their own day gives them one, and the verse reports their words without endorsing their sneer. On this reading too, the thousand years the confusion charge needs are gone, since a contemporary Harun stands inside Maryam's ﵍ own world. Al-Qummi's Harun is a wicked man and the exegetes' Harun is a saint, and the disagreement between the reports is real. The two readings still share one presupposition, that the name Harun sat on many men of her people, and that breadth of the name is what the naming custom rests on. A name forty thousand men carried sat on sinners and saints alike, and a crowd reaching for the house's name could reach for a notorious namesake or a holy one. blocks.text: Christian tradition traces the Lord's family to David, and Matthew opens his Gospel with the claim. Luke builds the Aaronic link into the infancy narrative through Elizabeth, as shown above. Helvidius, writing at Rome before 383, taught that the brothers named in Mark 6:3 were the Virgin's own sons by Joseph, and Jerome reports him so. Jerome answered that they were kin, the sons of Mary the wife of Alphaeus, called Mary of Clopas. He takes her for the sister or kinswoman of the Lord's mother, so that sons of the mother's sister can be called the Lord's brethren (Jerome, Against Helvidius, 383, chs. 14-16).
